title: Chapter 1: A Box From the Post Office
description: Chapter 1 of The Duck Who Stayed as a picture book to read aloud, a first draft, with the words on the pictures.
description_3d: Chapter 1 of The Duck Who Stayed as a paper book that opens and turns, a first draft.
audience: For children 5 to 8. A grown-up reads it to a child of 5 or 6. A child of about 7 reads it alone.

title_page.alt: The title page. On the right, Wren in a straw hat kneels on a kitchen floor and holds out her hands to Pip, a small white and grey robot duck.

spreads.title: The box
spreads.alt: A farmhouse kitchen. Aunt Mo walks in at the back door, carrying a cardboard box with a large red arrow on it pointing at the floor. Wren in her straw hat trots alongside with her nose level with the label. A bowl of apples is on the table and a chair stands by it.

p: On the very last hot day of summer, the truck came home from the post office with a box.
A box! With a name on it!
The name was not Wren. Wren felt this was a mistake.
“It has my name on it,” said Aunt Mo.
“You could share your name,” said Wren.
And what was inside?

spreads.title: Not yet
spreads.alt: The kitchen table, close, seen twice. On the left the box is still taped shut, with Wren's chin on the lid and Aunt Mo's hand flat on top. On the right the box is open and foam spills out, with a small flat beak poking up at an odd angle. Wren looks down at it, Grandpa Sol leans in at the door with his hammer, and Aunt Mo holds the scissors.

p: “Can we open it now?”
“Not yet.”
“Now?”
“Not yet.”
“How about now?”
Aunt Mo cut the tape. Wren stood on a chair. Foam. More foam. Foam, foam, foam. Then up poked one small flat beak.
“Pipped,” said Grandpa Sol. “Same as a chick coming through its shell.”
“Pip!” said Wren, quickly, before anyone had a different idea.

spreads.title: The goat
spreads.alt: The floor, seen from low down. Pip stands beside Grandpa Sol's boot, exactly as tall as the boot, with foam on one foot. Wren's finger comes in from the side, close to a green button on Pip's back. On the wall hangs a small framed drawing of a goat. Aunt Mo stands close by.

p: Out came Pip, all at once, no taller than Grandpa Sol’s boot.
“Does it lay?” asked Grandpa Sol.
“No,” said Aunt Mo.
“Then what’s it for?”
“I don’t know yet.”
Grandpa Sol nodded. He once had a goat like that.
Wren’s finger crept toward the green button.
“Not yet,” said Aunt Mo, and out came the manual.

spreads.title: The manual
spreads.alt: Aunt Mo stands behind a very large manual, held open with only her eyes showing over the top. Wren slumps on her elbows at the table, and a long neat row of apple cores runs along its edge. Pip stands switched off in the foam. Through the window, two hens go about their day.

p: Aunt Mo read page one. Wren ate an apple.
Page two. Wren ate an apple.
Page three. Wren ran out of apples.
“Keep Pip away from water,” read Aunt Mo.
“A duck,” said Grandpa Sol, “that keeps away from water.”
Nobody had anything to add.
“What does that page say?”
“It says, This page is blank.”
Wren thought about that for some time.

spreads.title: Hot soup
spreads.alt: The kitchen from floor height. Pip walks with its small careful steps along a dotted line that already bends away. Wren kneels with her arms out. A chair leg rises like a tree at the far right, and Aunt Mo's boots stand at the left edge.

p: “All right,” said Aunt Mo. “Now.”
Wren pressed once. Whirr. Up stood Pip.
Wren pressed twice. Tick, tick, tick.
Pip walked! It walked like someone carrying hot soup.
Wren ran ahead and knelt with her arms out.
“Come on, Pip! Come on!”
Tick, tick, tick.
A little to one side.
A little more to one side.
Past her hand...

spreads.title: CLONK
spreads.alt: Close and enormous. A chair leg fills the right page and Pip lies at its foot, flat on its side, legs in the air, with paper dust flying up. Huge cut-paper letters say the sound across both pages. Wren's two hands are at her mouth, and Aunt Mo's one raised finger comes in from the top.

p: Over went Pip, flat on its side, with both legs still going.
“It’s broken!” said Wren.
Aunt Mo held up one finger.
“Wait.”

spreads.title: Tuck, push, roll, up
spreads.alt: A comic strip of one floor, in two rows. In each row Pip tucks, pushes, rolls and stands, then walks to a chair leg. In the bottom row Wren has hauled the chair right to the far edge, wide-eyed, and the line of Pip's steps bends after it anyway. Aunt Mo stands behind her with her arms folded.

p: The legs stopped.
Tuck.
Push.
Roll.
Up!
Whirr. Tick, tick, tick.
And Pip walked into the very same chair leg.
Wren dragged the chair way over there.
Tuck.
Push.
Roll.
Up!
Whirr. Tick, tick, tick.
And Pip walked into a different leg.

spreads.title: That we can know
spreads.alt: The kitchen, full length. Wren and Aunt Mo face each other across Pip, who stands still on the floor between them. Wren points at the chair, and Aunt Mo holds the manual open with a thumb. The chair stands alone in the middle of the room, in nobody's way. Grandpa Sol is going out at the back door with his hammer, his back to us.

p: Aunt Mo pressed stop. Page twelve said: Pip does not look. Pip just goes.
“Pip doesn’t like that chair,” said Wren.
“We can’t know that,” said Aunt Mo.
“It went CLONK three times!”
“That we can know.”
Grandpa Sol went back to the hen house, looking pleased about something.

spreads.title: The green book
spreads.alt: Evening light in the kitchen. Wren holds the thin green book open at an empty page and looks across the whole room at Pip. Pip is on the shelf by the back door, plugged in, with one small light on. Aunt Mo leans at the table, and through the window the hens have still not been told.

p: Pip went on the shelf to charge.
“Can I show the hens?”
“Not yet.”
Out came a thin green book.
“This is blank,” said Wren.
“It’s a log. For what Pip did.”
“Can I put that Pip was mad?”
“Did you see mad?”
Wren looked. One small light, and nothing else.
She went to find a pencil.

spreads.title: Wren's log
spreads.alt: Wren writes at the table with Aunt Mo close beside her, a pen in her hand. Under the table the chair leg wears a bandage, and nobody mentions it. Pip charges on its shelf. On the right, a page of the green book holds Wren's log.

p: WREN’S LOG. Machine: Pip. Day 1.
Look: Pip walked into the chair leg. Two times.
Tried: Moved the chair. Pip walked into another leg. One time.
Told: Aunt Mo. Grandpa Sol. They were there.
Chair leg: fine. I checked.
Tomorrow: hens. They have not been told.
Not yet.
